events.title: Autoconf created
events.summary: David MacKenzie wrote the first Autoconf `configure` script in June 1991 — automating portability checks for GNU software builds.
events.about: Autoconf generates shell scripts that probe the host system for compilers, headers, and libraries — producing a `config.h` and Makefiles that build on Linux, BSD, and Solaris alike. It paired with Automake and Libtool as the GNU build triad for decades. Example: `./configure --prefix=/usr/local && make && make install` adapts to whatever the machine provides.

narrative.whyChosen: Autoconf ended hand-editing dozens of `-D` compiler flags for every Unix variant.
narrative.whyImportant: It became the standard way open-source C projects achieved portable builds before CMake dominated.
narrative.problemSolved: Maintainers could not test every platform; build scripts needed to discover capabilities at install time.

events.title: Phil Zimmermann releases PGP
events.summary: Phil Zimmermann released Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) 1.0 on June 5, 1991 — bringing public-key email encryption to activists and developers.
events.about: PGP let anyone encrypt email and files without a central authority — using RSA and IDEA in the first release. Zimmermann's export investigation made encryption policy a mainstream developer issue and paved the way for OpenPGP standards.

narrative.whyChosen: PGP democratized strong cryptography for ordinary computer users.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved end-to-end encryption could spread via grassroots distribution, not only government or corporate channels.
narrative.problemSolved: Email traveled in plaintext and proprietary crypto tools were unavailable to the public.
